digest.top_line: SIB-CRT in LARC: 9yr OS 74.3% vs 48.9% (HR 0.43, P=0.008) with a 56Gy PGTV boost, despite identical pCR (15.2% vs 18.4%).
digest.tldr: One lower-GI readout: a 106-pt randomized phase 2 says a simultaneous integrated boost to 56Gy buys 9-year OS, DFS, MFS and LC, but pCR did not move, so the mechanism for a ~25-point OS split is unexplained and MFS (HR 0.48) tracks LC (HR 0.40) too closely for a pelvic boost alone. Hypothesis-generating for dose escalation in chemo-naive LARC, not yet a reason to leave 50Gy/25fx.

sites.intro: Dose escalation in LARC, from an accrual window (2013-2015) that predates TNT, RAPIDO and PRODIGE-23.

studies.name: SIB-CRT vs Standard CRT for LARC (NCT02195141)
studies.tldr: 9yr OS 74.3% vs 48.9% (HR 0.43, P=0.008) with SIB dose escalation to 56Gy PGTV, despite identical pCR.
details: 🔍 Randomized phase 2, N=106 (55 SIB-CRT / 51 CRT), enrolled Aug 2013 to Feb 2015, median f/u 116.6mo
📐 RT: both arms 50Gy/25fx pelvis; SIB arm adds 56Gy to PGTV and 60Gy to lateral metastatic nodes when present
📊 pCR was NOT improved: 15.2% vs 18.4%, P=0.695, so the survival split is not mediated by pathologic downstaging
⚠️ MFS gain (HR 0.48) as large as LC gain (HR 0.40) is biologically hard to attribute to a pelvic boost
📊 Acute G3 toxicity 14.5% SIB-CRT vs 19.6% CRT, mostly radiation dermatitis
📊 Curative treatment (surgery or watch-and-wait) reached in 89.1% (49/55) vs 78.4% (40/51), P=0.135
⚠️ Benefit confined to the chemo-naive subgroup (9yr DFS 70.8%, HR 0.343, P=.014); no added benefit with periop chemo
⚠️ N=106 phase 2 with ~25-point absolute OS separation; effect size implausibly large for a boost alone, and OS/DFS were secondary
⚠️ 2013-2015 accrual predates TNT; both arms are pre-RAPIDO/PRODIGE-23 standards

verdict.rationale: Randomized phase 2, N=106, survival endpoints secondary; benefit driven by a chemo-naive subgroup and unexplained by the null pCR primary.
verdict.audience: Stage II/III rectal adenocarcinoma, neoadjuvant chemoradiation candidates

studies.significance: The primary endpoint (pCR) was flat, so the survival separation cannot be read as a downstaging effect, and LC (87.1% vs 70.1%) and MFS (70.8% vs 47.2%) moved together. That pattern, plus benefit only in chemo-naive pts, frames SIB to 56Gy as a boost worth testing where periop chemo is not deliverable, not a general escalation.
studies.monday_clinic: In stage II/III LARC pts who are not candidates for perioperative chemotherapy, this supports testing an SIB boost to the primary as a long-term-control strategy; it does not extend to pts receiving standard periop chemo, where no added benefit was seen.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Prospective **randomized phase 2** trial, 1:1, **N=106** (55 SIB-CRT, 51 CRT), accrued August 2013 to February 2015. Median follow-up **116.6 months**.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **Stage II/III rectal adenocarcinoma** planned for neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy. Radical surgery was planned **6 to 8 weeks** after chemoradiation.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Control arm: **50 Gy/25 fx** to the pelvis. Experimental arm: same 50 Gy/25 fx pelvis with **simultaneous integrated boost to 56 Gy to PGTV** and **60 Gy to lateral metastatic nodes** when present.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary: pCR rate.** Secondary: DFS, OS, MFS, local control, cancer-specific survival and toxicity.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: Acute grade 3 toxicity **14.5% (SIB-CRT) vs 19.6% (CRT)**, primarily radiation dermatitis. No late toxicity reported in source.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents stage II/III rectal adenocarcinoma treated with long-course neoadjuvant chemoradiation, particularly pts not receiving perioperative chemotherapy. Does not represent pts managed with total neoadjuvant therapy or short-course RT.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: The **primary endpoint was null** while every time-to-event secondary was positive, an internally inconsistent pattern for a boost acting through the pelvis. **Accrual closed in 2015**, before TNT became standard, and the subgroup that drove the benefit was defined by chemotherapy receipt, which was not randomized.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The escalation is modest and deliverable, 56 Gy SIB to PGTV inside a 50 Gy/25 fx pelvis, with acute G3 toxicity no worse (14.5% vs 19.6%). LC 87.1% vs 70.1% (HR 0.40) is the on-target signal; the equally large MFS gain (HR 0.48) is not, and that mismatch is the reason to treat this as hypothesis-generating rather than a reason to boost routinely.
significance_by_specialty.medonc: The interaction is the med onc read: SIB benefit was confined to pts who got no perioperative chemotherapy (9yr DFS 70.8%, HR 0.343, P=.014), with none added in those who did. That frames escalated RT as a substitute where systemic therapy cannot be delivered, not an addition on top of a standard chemo backbone.

papers.title: Dose-escalated versus Standard Neoadjuvant Chemoradiotherapy for Locally Advanced Rectal Cancer: 9-year Results of a Randomized Phase 2 Trial.
papers.journal: International journal of radiation oncology, biology, physics
papers.abstract:
PURPOSE: To compare the safety and efficacy of preoperative simultaneous integrated boost chemoradiotherapy (SIB-CRT) versus standard chemoradiotherapy (CRT) for locally advanced rectal cancer (LARC).

METHODS AND MATERIALS: This prospective, randomized phase II trial (NCT02195141) enrolled patients with stage II/III rectal adenocarcinoma. Patients were randomly assigned (1:1) to CRT (50 Gy/25 fx to pelvis) or SIB-CRT (50 Gy/25 fx to the pelvis with SIB of 56 Gy to PGTV and 60 Gy to lateral metastatic nodes if present). Radical surgery was planned 6-8 weeks after chemoradiotherapy. The primary endpoint was pathological complete response (pCR) rate; secondary endpoints were disease-free survival (DFS), overall survival (OS), metastasis-free survival (MFS), local control (LC), cancer-specific survival (CSS) and toxicity.

RESULTS: From August 2013 to February 2015, 106 patients were enrolled: 55 in the SIB-CRT group and 51 in the CRT group. Acute grade 3 toxicity occurred in 14.5% (SIB-CRT) and 19.6% (CRT) of patients, primarily manifested as radiation dermatitis. Curative treatment (radical surgery or watch-and-wait) was achieved in 89.1% (49/55) of SIB-CRT patients and 78.4% (40/51) of CRT patients (P=0.135). After a median follow-up of 116.6 months, the SIB-CRT group showed superior 9-year outcomes in the intention-to-treat (ITT) population: DFS (70.8% vs 47.4%; HR 0.46, P=0.013), OS (74.3% vs 48.9%; HR 0.43, P=0.008), MFS (70.8% vs 47.2%; HR 0.48, P=0.017), LC (87.1% vs 70.1%; HR 0.40, P=0.038) and CSS (77.4% vs 57.2%; P=0.027). Similar benefits were observed in the curative treatment cohort. The pCR rates were comparable (15.2% vs 18.4%; P=0.695). Exploratory subgroup analysis showed that the survival benefit of SIB-CRT was statistically significant in patients who did not receive perioperative chemotherapy (9-year DFS: 70.8%; HR=0.343, P = .014), whereas no additional benefit was observed in those receiving chemotherapy.

CONCLUSIONS: Dose escalation through SIB during neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy translates into superior long-term survival outcomes. Despite comparable pCR rates, the intensified control of both local disease and micrometastases by SIB-CRT, coupled with its significant superiority within the chemotherapy-naive subgroup, likely contributed to these robust results. These findings establish dose escalation as a potent strategy for optimizing long-term cure in the modern management of LARC, particularly in chemotherapy-ineligible patients.
